casos.name: v2.180.0: An Array of Reasonable Size
casos.body:
## node-opcua 2.180.0

**Compare:** [`v2.179.0...v2.180.0`](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/compare/v2.179.0...v2.180.0) · 3 commits · 2 pull requests

A small **hardening** release, published the day after 2.179.0. Two things: the binary decoder now refuses a message that declares an array longer than the bytes behind it, or nests recursive types without end; and a namespace default role permission configured through the public API is now actually enforced for remote sessions. The default behaviour of a server that configures neither is unchanged.

### ⚠️ Behaviour changes to review before upgrading

**Namespace default role permissions now apply to remote sessions.** A server that calls `namespace.setDefaultRolePermissions(...)`, or loads a nodeset that declares `DefaultRolePermissions`, will see that default enforced where it was previously ignored unless `setNamespaceMetaData()` was also called. A per-node `RolePermissions` still overrides the namespace default, and a server with no default configured keeps its permissive resolution. [0261e8739]

**Decode limits are on by default.** A message that declares an array of more than 1 048 576 elements on a structured-type field, an array the remaining bytes cannot hold, or more than 128 levels of nested `ExtensionObject`, `Variant` or `DiagnosticInfo`, is now rejected at decode time. Legitimate traffic is far below both ceilings (Part 6 §5.1.8 and §5.1.9 ask for at least 100 nesting levels). Both are static fields on `BinaryStream` and can be raised. [c2e0dfe85]

---

### 🛡️ Hardening

#### The decoder bounds what a message can ask for ([#1579](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1579))

The generic array decoder used by every structured-type array field looped over a wire-supplied `UInt32` length with no ceiling, and the three recursive types could nest without bound. `Variant` already had an array cap of its own; the generic path, the dynamic extension-object decoder and the recursive types did not.

- **`BinaryStream.maxArrayLength`** (default 1 MiB elements) and **`checkArrayLength()`**: an array length above the ceiling, or one that the remaining bytes cannot back since every element is at least one byte, is refused before anything is allocated. Wired into the generic `decodeArray` and the dynamic extension-object decoder.
- **A shared nesting budget**, `enterNestingLevel()` / `exitNestingLevel()` on `BinaryStream`, used by `DiagnosticInfo.decode`, `Variant.decode` and `decodeExtensionObject`. **`BinaryStream.maxNestingLevel`** defaults to 128. The counter is released on refusal, so a rejected message does not leak budget for the next one.
- **`ServerCapabilities.MaxArrayLength`** advertises the effective ceiling, the minimum of the configured value, the `Variant` cap and the generic cap, and the constructor raises the codec ceiling to cover a configured value larger than the default (raise-only).
- Tests in `node-opcua-binary-stream`, `node-opcua-basic-types` and `node-opcua-data-model`: array-length bounds, the nesting counter including the no-leak-on-refusal case, and an end-to-end nested `DiagnosticInfo` round trip.

#### Namespace default role permissions reach the enforcement path ([#1580](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1580))

When a node carries no `RolePermissions` of its own, Part 3 §5.2.9 resolves its access control from the namespace's `DefaultRolePermissions`. Two inconsistencies meant a default set through the public API never reached the permission check:

- **Configuration and enforcement read different places.** `Namespace.setDefaultRolePermissions()` stored the policy in a namespace field, and `BaseNode.getRolePermissions(inherited)` read it there, but `SessionContext.getApplicableRolePermissions` read the `DefaultRolePermissions` metadata node instead. The two were only connected when the operator also called `setNamespaceMetaData()`, which throws on a namespace loaded from a NodeSet2 file. The resolver now falls back to the namespace field when the metadata node is absent or Null, so both readers agree. Node-level and user-level precedence is preserved.
- **Initialization discarded declared values.** `ServerEngine.initialize()` reset every namespace's `DefaultRolePermissions` and `DefaultUserRolePermissions` property to Null, dropping any default a nodeset had declared. It now initializes only the unset properties to a readable Null and leaves a property that already carries a value alone.
- Tests: a namespace default reaches enforcement and a per-node `RolePermissions` still overrides it (confirmed to fail against the previous resolver); the same through a fully initialized `ServerEngine`; the existing permission suites stay green.

---

### 🚀 Features

- **server:** `unresolvedPermissionPolicy` is a documented `OPCUAServer` constructor option. It decides a remote session's permission when no `RolePermissions` apply at any level. The default stays `"allow"`, so nothing changes for existing servers; `"deny"` lets a deployment drive access entirely from declared policy. It was previously reachable only by assigning to the server field directly. [74c8ea58a]

```ts
const server = new OPCUAServer({
    unresolvedPermissionPolicy: "deny"   // default: "allow"
});
```

---

### Pull requests

- [#1579](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1579) Enforce a maximum array length and bound decode nesting depth
- [#1580](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1580) fix(address-space): honour namespace default role permissions on the enforcement path

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/compare/v2.179.0...v2.180.0
mensagens_commits:
feat(codec): enforce a maximum array length and bound decode nesting

The generic array decoder looped over a wire-supplied UInt32 length with no
ceiling, and ExtensionObject/Variant/DiagnosticInfo could nest with no limit.

Add BinaryStream.maxArrayLength plus checkArrayLength(), which also refuses a
length the remaining bytes cannot back, and wire it into the generic decodeArray
and the dynamic extension-object decoder. Add a shared nesting budget
(enterNestingLevel/exitNestingLevel) used by the three recursive decoders.

ServerCapabilities advertises the effective MaxArrayLength and raises the codec
ceiling to cover its configured value.

fix(address-space): honour namespace default role permissions on the enforcement path

setDefaultRolePermissions() wrote a private namespace field, but the permission
check read the DefaultRolePermissions metadata node instead, so a configured
namespace default only reached enforcement when setNamespaceMetaData() was also
called (which throws on NodeSet2-loaded namespaces). The resolver now falls back
to the namespace field, keeping it consistent with the local
getRolePermissions(inherited) getter.

ServerEngine.initialize() no longer overwrites a namespace's DefaultRolePermissions
Property when it already carries a value; it initializes only unset Properties to a
readable Null, so a default declared by a nodeset is preserved.

feat(server): expose unresolvedPermissionPolicy as an OPCUAServer option

The policy that decides a remote Session's permission when no RolePermissions
apply was only reachable by assigning to the server field directly. Surface it
as a documented constructor option. The default stays "allow", so behaviour is
unchanged; a deployment that drives access entirely from declared policy can now
pass unresolvedPermissionPolicy: "deny" to fail closed.

casos.name: v2.184.0: Modules, All The Way Down
casos.body:
# node-opcua 2.184.0: Modules, All The Way Down

**Compare:** [`v2.183.0...v2.184.0`](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/compare/v2.183.0...v2.184.0) · 93 commits · 48 pull requests · includes the `2.183.1` patch

> ### ⚠️ Read this first if your project is CommonJS
>
> **`node-opcua` is an ES module from this release.** 2.183.1 carried no `type` field; 2.184.0 declares `"type": "module"`.
>
> **Your application still runs.** `require("node-opcua")` works unchanged on the supported Node versions, and there is no `exports` map, so `main` and `types` resolve as they always did.
>
> **Your TypeScript build may stop compiling**, with `TS1479`, `TS1541` or `TS1542`, one per import site:
>
> ```
> error TS1479: The current file is a CommonJS module whose imports will produce 'require'
> calls; however, the referenced file is an ECMAScript module and cannot be imported with
> 'require'. Consider writing a dynamic 'import("node-opcua")' call instead.
> ```
>
> **The fix is one line in your `tsconfig.json`.** You do not convert your project to ESM, and it stays CommonJS:
>
> ```jsonc
> { "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext", "moduleResolution": "nodenext" } }
> ```
>
> That cures all three error codes at once. Confirmed on a real 145-file consumer: **258 errors to 0**, nothing else changed. Do not hand-fix `TS1541` with per-import `resolution-mode` attributes; it looks like progress and cannot finish the job.
>
> Full detail, including what converting to ESM would cost you instead, is under [If your build stops compiling](#if-your-build-stops-compiling) below.

## TL;DR

**Every one of the 122 packages is now a real ES module, the umbrella included.** node-opcua was written when CommonJS was the only option, and the whole workspace has just moved across in seven batches, from the eight leaf packages up through the encoding core, the address space, the client and server chain, and finally `node-opcua` itself. **Your application keeps running**: `require("node-opcua")` works exactly as it did, because Node has read ES modules from `require()` since 22.12 and the project has required 22.13 since last month. Two consumer fixtures, one CommonJS and one ESM, prove it on every single run. **A CommonJS TypeScript project does need one line changed** before it compiles again, and the banner above says which line.

**The toolchain moved with it.** The workspace compiles with TypeScript 7, which took a cold build from 192 seconds to 38, a real saving on every push since CI builds seven times before a test runs. Declaration maps ship now, so "go to definition" on a node-opcua symbol lands in the actual source instead of stopping at a `.d.ts`. Loading the SDK resolves a third fewer files after the generated nodeset packages stopped requiring 532 modules that contain nothing at run time. And five new gates check what npm actually publishes, which immediately found one companion nodeset package that had been shipping with no compiled code at all, and a sample command that had pointed at a deleted file for nearly three years.

**Alongside it, the alarm story continues and the test suite got honest.** Namespaces can now be deleted and repopulated, which takes a model recompile from 442 ms to single digits, the work behind an editor that stays warm. Alarms and Conditions clients finally get their condition filters answered, so the compliance tool's alarm collector runs at last, after reporting "no alarms received" for months. The suite itself now runs on Node's own type stripping rather than a transpiler, which stopped coverage being measured against compiled output nobody edits: the reported figure went from 79% to 91.7% without a single new test, because 32 500 covered lines had been counted against the wrong files.

---

### Highlights

- 📦 **122 of 122 packages are ESM.** `require("node-opcua")` is unaffected, proven by a CommonJS fixture on every run.
- ⚡ **TypeScript 7**: a cold workspace build drops from 192 s to 38 s.
- 🗺️ **Declaration maps ship**, so "go to definition" reaches the source.
- 🚀 **A third fewer files loaded**: `require("node-opcua")` goes from 1 606 files to 1 074.
- 🧹 **`deleteNamespace`**, so a model can be emptied and repopulated in milliseconds instead of rebuilding the address space.
- 🔔 **Condition filters work**: an empty-browsePath ConditionId operand resolves in both select and where clauses.
- 📊 **Coverage measured on the source**, 79% to 91.7%, no new tests.
- 🛡️ **Five packaging gates**, which found a package published with no code and a three-year-old broken command.

---

### If your build stops compiling

`node-opcua` declares `"type": "module"` from this release. 2.183.1 declared no `type` at all, so the umbrella went from format-neutral to ESM-only in one step. That is the change most likely to reach you, and it deserves more than a line.

**What still works, unchanged.** `require("node-opcua")` from a CommonJS file returns the module and every named export, because Node has read ES modules from `require()` without a flag since 22.12 and this project has declared a floor of 22.13 since 2.183.0. There is no `exports` map on the umbrella, so `main` and `types` resolve exactly as before. Verified directly: a CommonJS file requiring the published package resolves `OPCUAClient`, and `resolveNodeId("ns=0;i=85")` returns a real `NodeId`. The precondition for that is no module-scope `await` anywhere in the graph, which the `check:tla` gate has enforced since 2.181.0.

**What stops.** A CommonJS TypeScript project compiling against it reports one error per import site:

```
error TS1479: The current file is a CommonJS module whose imports will produce 'require'
calls; however, the referenced file is an ECMAScript module and cannot be imported with
'require'. Consider writing a dynamic 'import("node-opcua")' call instead.
```

The compiler is describing an older Node than you are running. Your project says CommonJS, the dependency says ESM, and under `module: node16` TypeScript still treats that pair as forbidden. It is a compile-time verdict, not a runtime one.

**Exactly one consumer shape breaks.** Both versions were installed from npm and driven through the same four projects, compiling and then running the emitted output:

| your project | with 2.183.1 | with 2.184.0 |
|---|---|---|
| plain JavaScript, `require("node-opcua")` | works | **works** |
| TypeScript, `module: commonjs` + `moduleResolution: node` | works | **works** |
| TypeScript, `module: node16` | works | **TS1479** |
| TypeScript, `module: nodenext` | works | **works** |

**The fix is `nodenext`, and your project stays CommonJS:**

```jsonc
{ "compilerOptions": { "module": "nodenext", "moduleResolution": "nodenext" } }
```

`nodenext` is the setting that knows a modern Node can `require()` an ES module; `node16` is the one that does not. You do not add `"type": "module"`, you do not rewrite imports, and you do not switch to `await import()`. The compiler keeps emitting CommonJS: with `nodenext`, `tsc` emits `const node_opcua_1 = require("node-opcua")` and the result runs.

This was confirmed on a real consumer, not only on a probe. A 145-file package with 19 node-opcua dependencies went from **258 errors to 0** with those two settings and nothing else changed, and its full pipeline then ran end to end.

**Three error codes, one cause.** The same upgrade produces `TS1479` on value imports, `TS1541` on type-only imports and `TS1542`. In that 145-file package the split was 180, 76 and 2. **All three are cured by the one line above.** `TS1541` is a trap worth naming: it suggests a per-import `resolution-mode` attribute, which appears to work, so you can spend an afternoon hand-editing a third of the errors before discovering that `TS1479` next door cannot be fixed that way at all.

**Converting to ESM also works, and costs much more.** The moment you set `"type": "module"` your own code inherits ESM specifier strictness: every relative import needs an explicit `.js`, measured at **513 rewrites across 107 files** in that same package. Extensionless subpaths into node-opcua packages, such as `node-opcua-address-space/nodeJS`, also stop resolving. Under `nodenext`-as-CommonJS both keep working, because these packages publish no `exports` map and CommonJS still guesses extensions. The cost of converting is not one setting, it is every import you own.

**One caveat if you are on TypeScript 5.** `moduleResolution: "node"` ignores both `type` and `exports`, so a project on that setting compiles today with no change at all. That is not a long-term answer, since TypeScript 7 removed it outright (`TS5108`), but it explains why some packages in one workspace break and others do not.

**If the errors do not go away, delete the build cache.** This is the most likely reason you will think the fix failed. With `incremental: true`, which `composite: true` implies, TypeScript caches diagnostics per file and a change in an *extended* `tsconfig.json` does not invalidate them, so old files replay old errors. Run `tsc -b --force`, or delete every `.tsbuildinfo`. Note that when `outDir` is set the cache lives **inside the output directory**, not beside your `tsconfig.json`, so deleting the file you expect to find achieves nothing. Reproduced: `node16` gives one `TS1479`; switching to `nodenext` and deleting `./tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` still gives one; deleting `out/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo` gives zero, with no source change.

**Bundlers: most are fine, and the exception is not about ES module support.** What matters is whether your bundler emits the `require()` and lets Node resolve it, or pre-validates the externalisation against a rule that predates Node 22.12. esbuild is verified working, externalising the whole family from a CommonJS output with a 658-test suite passing. **Next.js 16.2.6 with Turbopack is confirmed broken**: it refuses to externalise an ES module, bundles it instead, and the build then dies because those packages were externalised precisely for using `__dirname` and reading nodeset files from disk. Its message says "The package seems invalid", which describes its own check rather than the package, and no node-opcua change can fix it.

**For scale**, in the 22-package workspace where all of this was measured, twenty-one packages upgraded untouched: a CLI, a language server, an editor extension and several back-end services. One Next.js application broke.

The full guide, with the FAQ and the measurements, is at [documentation/migrating_to_esm.md](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/blob/master/documentation/migrating_to_esm.md).

---

### ⚠️ Behaviour changes to review before upgrading

**Every package is an ES module, the umbrella included.** `"type": "module"` on all 122, where 2.183.1 declared none. Nothing changes at run time, and a CommonJS TypeScript project needs one line changed to compile. See [If your build stops compiling](#if-your-build-stops-compiling). [#1690](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1690) through [#1704](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1704)

**A project compiling against node-opcua needs TypeScript 5.0 or above.** The generated nodeset indexes now use `export type *`, which is TypeScript 5.0 syntax and appears in published `.d.ts` files that `node-opcua-address-space` re-exports. TypeScript 4.x cannot parse them. TypeScript 5.0 is from March 2023 and the Node floor is already 22.13. [#1688](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1688)

**Hand-run scripts are renamed to `.cjs`.** Roughly 40 CommonJS scripts across `bin/` and playground directories keep their CommonJS form under an explicit extension. Three published commands moved with their manifest entries, so nothing a consumer types changes. The end-to-end tests that spawn a server *by file name* were updated, a reference no compiler or gate can see. [#1701](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1701) [#1703](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1703) [#1704](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1704)

**`node-opcua-samples` generates its certificate folder as CommonJS.** `node-opcua-pki` writes a CommonJS `certificates/config.js` and then requires it; once the package became a module that file was read as ESM and `pki` failed while still exiting 0. A `certificates/package.json` carrying `{"type":"commonjs"}` scopes the generated folder back. [#1704](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1704)

**Fourteen type re-exports became `export type`.** `export { SomeInterface } from "..."` is elided by a whole-program compiler and kept by a single-file transpiler, where it becomes a link error under ESM. Five were in the `node-opcua` and `node-opcua-client` entry points, so they would have failed to link for any ESM consumer. `isolatedModules` is now on across the workspace, so the class cannot return. [#1710](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1710)

**A test file with `#` in its name is renamed.** ESM resolves a specifier as a URL, so `#804.js` was read as a fragment and discarded. It was the only such file in the repository, and the gate now reports `#` and `?` in a relative specifier. [#1711](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1711)

**Every Variable created by one nodeset load carries the same `sourceTimestamp`.** One clock reading is taken per load and reused, keyed on the address space being loaded and reference counted, so a server writing elsewhere or outside a load still gets a real clock. [#1728](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1728)

**A state machine type declares the transition event it raises.** node-opcua's finite state machines raise a `TransitionEventType` on every state change, but no `GeneratesEvent` reference said so, which OPC 10000-16 requires and the compliance tool checks on every state machine instance. One reference is added to `FiniteStateMachineType`, covering every subtype. One catalog digest moves with it. [#1705](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1705)

**A semantics change raises `SemanticChangeEventType` on the Server object**, alongside the SemanticsChanged bit, as OPC 10000-5 6.4.31 requires. The bit itself no longer becomes part of the change-detection baseline, which used to produce a second, bit-less notification for a value that never changed. [#1706](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1706)

**Coverage numbers move for measurement reasons, not code reasons.** The suite runs on Node's own type stripping, so coverage lands on the TypeScript sources instead of compiled output. The reported figure goes from 79.06% to 91.70% with the same tests: 32 500 lines were always covered and were being counted against files nobody edits. [#1714](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1714)

---

### 🚀 The ESM migration (FEAT-2)

Seven batches, ordered by dependency layer rather than by size, because a CommonJS package sitting on top of flipped ones is the dangerous position: under a transpiling test loader it duplicates every module beneath it, and anything holding module-level state splits in two silently.

| batch | packages | running total |
|---|---|---|
| [#1690](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1690) | 8 leaves, then 22 more (the `service-*` family and friends) | 30 |
| [#1692](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1692) | the 31 generated companion nodeset packages | 61 |
| [#1694](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1694) | the encoding and data core, 18 packages | 81 |
| [#1696](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1696) | the bottom layer, 11 packages | 93 |
| [#1699](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1699) | `leak-detector`, the last hand-written CommonJS package | 94 |
| [#1701](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1701) | `address-space` and its neighbours, 7 packages | 101 |
| [#1703](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1703) | the client and server chain, and the umbrella, 12 packages | 113 |
| [#1704](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1704) | the last nine | **122 of 122** |

Three findings worth carrying away:

- **Batch 3 failed CI with 10 000 type errors**, all cascading from a generator that had quietly written nothing. The cause was two copies of `node-opcua-factory`: the built-in type registry is filled by import side effects, and the last CommonJS package in that chain made the test loader create a second module object with its own state, so `NumericRange` registered into the copy nobody read. The generator now exits non-zero when it cannot resolve a schema, instead of logging and returning.
- **The umbrella could not lag behind the packages it re-exports.** Flipping `client` and `server` alone broke ESM consumers only: Node discovers a CommonJS module's named exports with a static lexer that can see through other CommonJS files, and once the re-export targets became ES modules the names simply vanished. `require("node-opcua")` never broke, because it reads an object at run time rather than resolving names before evaluation.
- **`tsc -b` does not re-emit on a `type` change alone**, so an ordinary build leaves CommonJS output and looks like it worked. Every batch verified the emitted files rather than trusting the build.

---

### 🏗️ Modernisation

**TypeScript 7** ([#1693](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1693)). A cold `tsc -b packages` goes from 192 s to 38 s, and `build:all` from CI's 152 to 224 s down to 51 s. The output was compared rather than assumed: of 2 584 emitted JavaScript files **2 differ**, by redundant parentheses around an identifier, and 6 declaration files differ by union member order and character escaping. The checkers under `tools/` read the classic compiler API, which TypeScript 7 does not expose, so they depend on a `typescript-5` alias that also names, at the import site, which compiler is meant.

**A third fewer files at load** ([#1688](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1688)). The generated nodeset packages are mostly type declarations: 536 of 576 compiled modules in `node-opcua-nodeset-ua` have no run-time content, and `export *` loaded them anyway.

| require | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `node-opcua-address-space` | 1 297 files | 765 |
| `node-opcua` | 1 606 files | 1 074 |

**Declaration maps** ([#1702](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1702)). 2 628 maps, every one verified to resolve to a file that exists. `dist` grows about 2%, build time is unchanged.

**Five new gates.** Each answers a different question about what is published, and each was verified against the defect it exists to catch rather than merely observed green:

| gate | question |
|---|---|
| `check-build-graph` ([#1698](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1698)) | is the package compiled at all? |
| `check-package-shape` ([#1700](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1700)) | is the manifest coherent, do a consumer's imports resolve? (publint and attw) |
| `check-cjs-globals` ([#1711](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1711)) | does an ES module reference `require`, `module` or `exports`? |
| `check-erasable` ([#1718](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1718)) | will Node's type stripping refuse this file? |
| `check-c8-ignore` ([77c3feb50]) | are the coverage hints in the form c8 reads? |

What they found immediately: **`node-opcua-nodeset-i-4-aas` was published with no compiled code at all**, missing from the aggregate build list, and `check-pack` had been blind to it because `main: "dist/index.js"` does not start with `./` and was read as a bare specifier. 37 of 115 packages write their entry points that way. `node-opcua-leak-detector` had been shipping without its types. The `convert-nodeset-to-javascript` CLI had no shebang, so it was not executable on Linux. And the `simple_client` command has pointed at a file deleted in November 2023. [#1695](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1695) [#1707](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1707)

**The test suite runs on Node's own type stripping** ([#1714](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1714), [#1710](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1710), [#1715](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1715)). Two resolver redirects replace the transpiler, with `TSX=1` as a fallback. No import is rewritten and no experimental flag is used. Coverage lands on the sources, and `c8` finally reads its own configuration: the previous file was an `nyc` YAML file that c8 ignored silently, so none of its settings had ever applied and `--all` was reporting 3 103 never-loaded source files at 0%.

---

### 🚀 Features

- **`deleteNamespace(indexOrUri)`** empties a namespace and frees its index for reuse, so a tool that recompiles a model does not have to rebuild the whole address space. Deleting node by node used to leave survivors: a DataType or a ReferenceType could not be deleted at all, so on the AutoID nodeset 15 nodes threw and 15 survived. The delete batches its model-change transaction instead of opening one per node, which is where most of the gain is. Measured on that nodeset: a full rebuild is 442 ms, the old node-by-node loop 89 ms, and `deleteNamespace` 4 to 8 ms, or 3.8 ms with the new `suspendModelChangeEvents` option. `modelChangeTransaction` is published too, so a caller can batch its own work the same way. [#1726](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1726)
- **`registerNodePromoter` accepts a NodeId**, so an application can register a promoter for a type it defines itself or for a companion-specification type, whose namespace index is a property of the load rather than a constant. The numeric form still works. Shipped in 2.183.1. [#1684](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1684)
- **`onSetpointDataValueChange`**, the deviation-alarm counterpart of `onInputDataValueChange`, completing the alarm extension points published in 2.183.0. Shipped in 2.183.1. [#1682](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1682)
- **`trustSiblingImages`** (opt-in, off by default) skips the read-and-hash that proves a precompiled nodeset image matches its XML, checking the recorded source length against the file size instead. The bargain is explicit: an edit that changes the length is still caught, one that keeps it byte-for-byte is not. [#1728](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1728)

---

### ⚡ Performance

Beyond the build and load figures above, two passes over the address space, both measured with pinned process priority because a laptop migrating a benchmark between performance and efficiency cores reports regressions that are not there:

- **The loader stops reading scanning getters per node.** `findReferences` calls during a standard-plus-DI load drop from 10 136 to 6 132, and `findReferencesAsObject` from 4 898 to 894. Image node decoding loses two allocations per node. [#1728](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1728)
- **One chain walk answers three DataType questions.** `_getDefinition` asked separately whether a type was an Enumeration, a Structure and a Union, each walking the supertype chain; and `isSubtypeOf`'s memo is invalidated by every `HasSubtype` reference added anywhere, so during a load it is thrown away before it is read. `allReferences` calls drop from 2 966 to 236, and the median warm load by about 10%. [#1729](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1729)

That PR also carries **a correction and a negative result**, both worth more than the speedup. The work was opened on a profile claiming one function was 59% of a load; a warm profile, taken around the loads rather than the process, puts it at 3.9%, and the PR says so in its first paragraph. And four routes through image parsing were measured to close the question of whether string slicing was costing anything: the current route is already the fastest available, and the ceiling is 9% for a format change.

---

### 🐛 Fixes

#### Alarms and Conditions, and the compliance tool

- **service-filter:** an empty `browsePath` in a `SimpleAttributeOperand` denotes the instance itself, per Part 4 §7.4.4.5, not "nothing to resolve". Every Alarms and Conditions client asks for the ConditionId with exactly that operand, so the select clause came back `BadNothingToDo`, the compliance tool's alarm collector gave up, and every A&C unit was skipped. [#1716](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1716)
- **service-filter:** the same rule now applies to where clauses, so `InList(ConditionId, ...)` and `Equals` match the event's own ConditionId. Measured before the fix: a wide monitored item received 3 condition events, a filtered one on the same subscription received 0. Delivery and evaluation now share one resolver so they cannot drift apart again. [#1717](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1717)
- **server:** the SemanticsChanged bit reaches the notification the client actually reads. The stamped notification used to be appended behind whatever was already queued, and the bit was stored in the change-detection baseline, which produced a spurious second notification. Nine compliance scripts go from error or warning to passing. [#1706](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1706)
- **address-space:** a state machine type declares `GeneratesEvent` to `TransitionEventType`. [#1705](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1705)

#### Address space

- **address-space:** the declared parent names the node. The NodeIdManager named a new node from its inverse aggregating references only, so a folder that a type merely organizes got a half-chained symbolic name, and a modeler seeding ids from a working group's table could not match it. `instantiate()` now forwards `parentNodeId` too. Shipped in 2.183.1. [#1683](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1683)
- **address-space:** an `enumValues` entry keeps its description. The array form of `addMultiStateValueDiscrete` built each `EnumValueType` from the display name and value only, silently dropping a description the type declares. [#1723](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1723)
- **conformance:** the hand-built ArrayItemType properties are named in namespace 0, so a client translating the standard browse path no longer gets `BadNoMatch`; the analog array items accept a write to `EngineeringUnits`. [#1706](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1706)

#### Tests and infrastructure

- **leak-detector:** the registry check was called with one argument too many, so the quiet path was unreachable and every block was judged on whether anything anywhere in the process had ever leaked. One abandoned object took down 42 unrelated tests, and in a single-process run of the whole suite it produced 293 failures. After the fix: 3, all environmental. [#1712](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1712)
- **enum:** a benchmark comparison asserted our implementation is fastest, from an unawaited async handler, so a timing inversion on a loaded runner escaped as an unhandled rejection and took the runner down with four suites in flight. A real failure in that file now names itself instead of hiding behind a timeout. [#1727](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1727)
- **address-space:** the shelving test raced its own unshelve timer with a 300 ms margin, and its assertions ran inside a listener where a failure could not reach mocha. [#1709](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1709)
- **discovery:** a test asserted an exact count of mDNS announcements while listening to the whole subnet, which is an assertion that nothing else on the network is announcing. It counts its own uniquely named announcement now. [#1720](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1720)
- **discovery:** an LDS restart on a fixed port raced the operating system releasing the socket, which read as an unrelated flake on Node 24. [#1697](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1697)
- **generator:** the scratch entry point is deleted (15 lines, no references, and the function it called always threw), and the dynamic imports on the deprecated schema path take a file URL, since an absolute Windows path begins with something the ESM loader reads as a URL scheme. [#1724](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1724)
- **ci:** the API documentation is curated by major and minor line, keeping the latest patch, so the Pages artifact stays under its size limit. [#1685](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1685)

---

### 🗑️ Housekeeping

169 dead CommonJS files are deleted: 162 schema literals from 2015 in thirteen `service-*` packages, three `nyc` configs, three unreferenced fixtures and one explorer script. None was published, and one search across the whole repository found every reference inside the deleted set itself. [#1686](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1686)

A new gate refuses an import that reaches into another package's `impl/` directory. The current count is zero, which is the cheap moment to add one: a gate introduced after the count grows is a negotiation. [#1725](https://github.com/node-opcua/node-opcua/pull/1725)

---

### 📦 Dependencies

TypeScript moves from 5.9.3 to **7.0.2**, with a `typescript-5` alias kept for the tools that read the classic compiler API and for `node-opcua-generator`, which compiles generated code at run time. `c8` is pinned at 12.0.0 as a devDependency instead of being fetched unpinned on every invocation, and `publint` and `@arethetypeswrong/cli` join the packaging gates. `typedoc` leaves the root devDependencies, since both callers invoke it through `pnpx`, which resolves its own compiler.

Static reference search cannot prove a file unused when it can be loaded by

because of the type-position bug fixed alongside this.

fix(service-discovery): import Bonjour by name in the test

Under ESM the default import of a CommonJS dependency is its module.exports
object, not the class, so `new Bonjour()` stopped type-checking once this
package flipped. The source already used the named export.

build(nodesets): generate the companion packages as ESM

The generator writes "type": "module" into every manifest it emits, and all
31 companion packages are regenerated. They are type declarations plus a
few enums, so nothing else in them changes: the regeneration produced no
source diff at all.

build: compile with TypeScript 7

A cold `build:all` drops from about 200s to about 50s, and the emitted JavaScript
is identical across all 2584 files except redundant parentheses in two of them.
The checkers under tools/ and node-opcua-generator use the classic compiler API,
which TypeScript 7 does not expose, so they keep a 5.9.3 copy under the name
typescript-5: the workspace allows one version per module name, and the alias
says at the import site which compiler is meant.

Two latent config bugs surfaced. node-opcua-types/tsconfig.pre.json spelled "no
inputs of its own" as include [""], which TypeScript 5 read as nothing and
TypeScript 7 reads as the whole package. check-test-types resolved
typescript/bin/tsc, a subpath TypeScript 7's exports map does not publish.

build: flip the encoding core to ESM (FEAT-2 batch 3)

basic-types, binary-stream, nodeid, data-model, data-value, date-time,
numeric-range, status-code, variant, extension-object, factory, schemas,
types, json, like-matcher, chunkmanager, utils and common. Tool-generated,
plus three test anchors and the build-time one in types/source/generate.ts.

fix(check-import-extension): see `import(...)` in a type position

TypeScript parses `const x: import("./thing").Thing` as an ImportTypeNode
rather than the dynamic-import call the gate already knew, so an
extensionless one reached the compiler as TS2835 instead of the gate.

fix(common): give an inline type import its extension

Found by the gate fix above, once node-opcua-common became ESM.

build: flip node-opcua-generator, and let the generator fail loudly

Under tsx, a CommonJS package transpiles the ESM dist it imports into a
second copy, so the type registry existed twice and the built-in types
registered into the one nobody read. Flipping the last CommonJS link in
that chain leaves one instance. The generate script now exits non-zero.

fix(pack): a path without ./ is still a path, and ship what it names

check-pack skipped any entry point not starting with "." or "/", reading it as a
bare specifier redirecting to another package. Only an exports target has that
form, so the rule silently exempted main/types in 37 of 115 packages. Among them
node-opcua-nodeset-i-4-aas, which is missing from packages/tsconfig.json, is
therefore never built, and ships on npm with no dist at all: 2.183.1 contains
only LICENSE, package.json and 44 source files while main names dist/index.js.

Adds the missing project reference, publishes the two root entry files of
node-opcua-leak-detector (files listed only src/, so types never shipped), and
restricts the bare-specifier exemption to exports targets.

test(discovery): wait for the port before starting another LDS

shutdown() resolves before the OS releases the listening socket, so a test
that restarts the LDS on the same port raced that release and failed with
EADDRINUSE on 2516. It is a race, so it passed on node 22 and failed on 24,
reading as an unrelated flake.

fix(debug): read the module filename the way ESM provides it

The log label tested `typeof __filename`, which is always undefined once
this package is an ES module, so the branch carrying the real value was
dead. import.meta.filename is undefined in browser bundles, so the
placeholder fallback stays.

chore(debug): name the hand-run script .cjs

bin/raw_to_hex.js is CommonJS, is not declared as a bin and nothing
references it. In an ESM package it would be parsed as a module.

build: flip the bottom layer to ESM (FEAT-2 batch 4)

debug, nodesets, test-helpers, test-fixtures, versions, data-access and
alias-name-common had no CommonJS dependency left, and flipping debug
unblocks address-space-base, pseudo-session, xml2json and packet-analyzer,
which go with them. Ordered by dependency layer, after the batch 3 lesson.

feat(tools): check that every publishable package is actually built

`tsc -b packages` builds the projects packages/tsconfig.json references and,
transitively, the ones those reference. That aggregate list is maintained by hand:
fix-tsconfigs rewrites each package's own references, nothing writes the aggregate.
A package outside the closure is never compiled, which is how
node-opcua-nodeset-i-4-aas reached npm carrying only its sources.

check-pack catches that shape at pack time; this catches the cause, and since it
only reads files it runs inside lint:ci. Private packages are exempt: playground
sits outside the graph on purpose.

fix(esm-convert): a createRequire require is not CommonJS left behind

The tool writes that form itself when it converts a require it cannot turn
into an import, then reported the result as needing a decision.

build(leak-detector): port the last hand-written CommonJS to ESM

index.js, the two src modules and the 11 spawned fixtures, plus the mocha
config rename. wtfnode stays behind createRequire: it is loaded only on
demand and must stay synchronous, since a module-scope await would break
require(esm) for CommonJS consumers. index.js was also missing from files.

test(leak-detector): run mocha directly, not through npx

These tests time the child to prove a leaked handle does not stop a process
exiting, and npx spent 8.5 to 10.3 seconds resolving a binary before mocha
started, which is the whole budget of those assertions. The suite now takes
11 seconds instead of 2 minutes, and measures the thing under test.

feat(tools): gate the published shape with publint and attw

check-pack proves a promised file is in the tarball; it cannot say the promise is
wrong. publint reads the packed manifest, attw resolves the package as both an ESM
and a CommonJS consumer. attw runs under the esm-only profile, so the deliberate
"CommonJS consumers use require(esm)" stance is not reported as a fault.

Ratcheted like check-test-types: six packages are grandfathered, four of them the
named-exports shape that the ESM flip removes on its own. The seventh failure is
fixed here instead, a missing shebang that left the convert-nodeset CLI
non-executable on Linux.

chore(address-space): name the nodeset CLI scripts .cjs

Four hand-written CommonJS scripts, two of them published commands. They
run under plain node, where require(esm) loads the ESM dist in one
instance, so renaming is enough and porting 1143 lines of CLI is not.

build: flip address-space and its neighbours to ESM (FEAT-2 batch 5)

address-space, secure-channel, certificate-manager, client-proxy, modeler,
role-set-common and alias-name-server. address-space matters most: leaving
it CommonJS on top of 94 ESM packages is the arrangement that duplicated a
module registry in batch 3.

chore: name the hand-run sample scripts .cjs

aggregates/bin/sample_aggregate_server and the two model/bin extractors are
CommonJS, declared as neither bin nor files, and run by hand under node.

build: flip the client and server chain, and the umbrella (FEAT-2 batch 6)

client, server, aggregates, server-discovery, vendor-diagnostic, model,
convert-nodeset-to-javascript, address-space-for-conformance-testing,
role-set-client, role-set-server, alias-name-client and node-opcua itself.
The umbrella has to move with them: see the PR for what breaks otherwise.

build: emit declaration maps

"Go to definition" on a node-opcua symbol lands in the generated .d.ts and stops
there, which is the shape of the declaration rather than the code that produced it.
declarationMap sends the editor on to the .ts, which the packages already publish
beside their dist for the same reason sourceMap is on.

2628 maps, every one resolving to a source file that exists; dist grows from 135 MB
to 138 MB. The maps for a few test-helper directories point at sources that are not
published, which is what their .js.map already does.

fix: state machine types declare GeneratesEvent -> TransitionEventType

FEAT-57: the CTT's Base Info State Machine Instance script walks each
StateMachine instance's type up to StateMachineType looking for a
forward GeneratesEvent reference, and fails when none is found. The
standard nodeset cannot declare this on our behalf since it depends on
what a server actually raises, and node-opcua's finite state machines
always raise TransitionEventType on a state change.

Add the reference once on FiniteStateMachineType, from every state
machine's post-initialize step, idempotently, so it covers every
subtype (ExclusiveLimitStateMachineType included) the CTT's walk can
reach. Refresh the adi nodeset catalog digest fixture, which now picks
up the two extra references from a state machine instantiated at load.

fix(esm-convert): keep the shebang on line 1

The createRequire preamble was inserted above it, which is TS18026 and
stops the script being executable. Two node-opcua-samples bin scripts
failed to compile before this was caught.

build: flip the last nine packages to ESM (FEAT-2 batch 7)

end2end-test, samples, playground, local-discovery-server, file-transfer,
alias-name-test, role-set-test, role-set-admin and client-browser. 29
hand-run and spawned scripts become .cjs, including five test servers the
end-to-end suite names by string. The workspace is now 122 of 122.

fix(samples): keep the generated certificate folder CommonJS

node-opcua-pki writes a CommonJS certificates/config.js and then requires
it. With this package ESM that file was parsed as ESM, so generation failed
with "module is not defined" while pki still exited 0, leaving every suite
that needs a certificate to fail on a missing .pem.

fix(end2end): point the last spawned server at its .cjs name

One reference kept the old .js name: my rename swept [a-z_]+ and this file
is the one whose name carries capitals. The suite reported it honestly as
"cannot find server script".

fix(server): a semantic change stamps the notifications already queued

OPC 10000-4 7.39 wants the next data change notification to carry the
SemanticsChanged bit. When notifications are still queued - the initial
value of a freshly created monitored item above all - that next
notification is one of them, not a new sample, so appending a fresh one
leaves the client's first notification bit-less and repeats a value that
never changed.

CTT Data Access Semantic Changes 003/004/005/010/013 create the item,
write the Property and publish once, reading the bit off
MonitoredItems[0]: the queued initial value. They failed with
"Expected <16384> but got <0>" while the delivered pair was 0x0, 0x4000.

The pending queue is stamped instead, over every sampling interval,
timestamps and filter combination.

fix(conformance): ArrayItemType properties are named in namespace 0

The mandatory Properties of ArrayItemType - Title, EURange,
EngineeringUnits, InstrumentRange, AxisScaleType and the axis
definitions - are declared in namespace 0, so their BrowseName is
0:EURange. The five hand-built ArrayItemType nodes of the CTT folder
named them in the simulator's own namespace instead, and a client
translating the standard browse path got BadNoMatch.

That is what CTT Data Access Semantic Changes 014-017 reported as
"Mandatory property 'EURange' missing in configured node".

fix(server): the SemanticsChanged bit never becomes part of the value

The bit marks one notification (OPC 10000-4 7.39), but _enqueue_value stored the
stamped DataValue as oldDataValue - the baseline the next sample is compared
against. That sample then differed by StatusCode alone, so the item reported a
second, bit-less data change for a value that never changed, and with the queue
size of 1 the CTT asks for that duplicate is what the client reads.

It is why stamping the pending queue fixed Semantic Changes 003/004/005, whose
queue is not empty, and not AnalogItemType 008 or Semantic Changes 010/013 and
014-017, which drain the queue first: those all got the duplicate.

The notification is built before the bit is cleared, and apply_timestamps hands
back a fresh DataValue, so the queued notification keeps it.

feat(address-space): a semantics change also raises SemanticChangeEventType

OPC 10000-5 6.4.31 has the Server report a semantics change twice: the
SemanticsChanged bit for whoever monitors the DataItem, and a
SemanticChangeEventType on the Server object, naming the affected Node and its
TypeDefinition, for whoever monitors the Server. Only the bit was implemented.

It is raised from handle_semantic_changed, the one point every semantics change
already goes through, so the event and the bit cannot disagree. Modelled on how
the address space raises GeneralModelChangeEventType.

CTT Base Info SemanticChange 001 subscribes to both and reported "No
EventNotification has been received of node ... after a write has been issued".

fix(conformance): the analog array items accept a write to EngineeringUnits

addAnalogDataItem builds EngineeringUnits read-only while EURange and
InstrumentRange are writable. A CTT run has to be able to change all three.

Data Access Semantic Changes 013 writes the three properties of the six
AnalogItemType Arrays items in one Write. BadNotWritable is on its accepted
list, but it then nulls those six entries and reuses the full-length
expected-results array for its revert write, which its own WriteHelper refuses:
"ExpectedOperationResultsArray[] (length: 18) must have the same size as
Request.NodesToWrite[] (length: 12)".

Set where the test nodes are configured, rather than changing what
addAnalogDataItem gives every other server.

test(address-space): the event listener takes IEventData

The listener was typed from what the test reads out of the event and
returned the push count, which master's stricter signature refuses.

fix(samples): point simple_client at the script it was renamed to

bin.simple_client named ./dist/simple_client_ts.js, which stopped existing in
November 2023 when commit 1cba6e96e renamed the example: bin/simple_client.js became
bin/client_example.js (now .cjs) and bin/simple_client_ts.ts became
bin/client_example_ts.ts. The manifest kept the old path, so every release since has
installed a simple_client command pointing at nothing.

It now names bin/client_example.cjs, the direct rename of the file the command was
built on, with a node shebang. The compiled sibling carries "#!/usr/bin/env tsx" and
would ask a consumer for tsx.

fix(end2end): name a test file without a URL-reserved character

ESM resolves a specifier as a URL, so `...source_issue#804.js` is read as a
path with a `#804.js` fragment and the module is reported missing, while
CommonJS treated `#` as an ordinary character. check-import-extension now
reports `#` and `?` in a specifier: the extension is right, so no other rule
looked.

feat(tools): add check-cjs-globals gate for CommonJS globals in ESM files

Flags require/module/exports used as a value in a .ts/.js file that is
an ES module, resolving bindings (createRequire, parameters, locals)
through the TypeScript AST rather than a regex. --fix rewrites the one
safe idiom, if (require.main === module), to the import.meta.url form.

Also fixes two dead references to the CommonJS exports object found
by the new gate in node-opcua-generator, and a pre-existing formatting
issue in one of the two already-converted sample servers that blocked
lint:ci.

test(address-space): stop the shelving test racing its own unshelve timer

The unshelveTime sampler ran every 400ms against a 1500ms shelve, so the
third sample (the minimum the test asserts) had under 300ms of slack and a
loaded CI machine produced only two. Sample every 200ms instead.

Assertions also ran inside the value_changed listener and the sampling
timer, where a failure escapes mocha as an uncaught exception and leaves
the promise pending; they now run after the await.

test(end2end): wait for the data, not for a keepalive, in the 5000-node test

A keepalive is only sent on a publish cycle with nothing to report, and 5000
items on continuously changing Scalar_Simulation_* variables rarely leave one.
Anything that slows the backlog down - c8, a loaded machine - filled those gaps
and the 5s budget expired.

Wait instead for data from every monitored item, which is what the assertions
that follow are about.

fix(leak-detector): report what a block leaked, not what the process accumulated

start() called verify_registry_counts(self, info) with one argument too many, so
`info` was `self`, `info.silent` was undefined and the check could never stay
quiet. Once anything anywhere in the process had leaked, every later start()
threw LEAKS !!! from a `before` hook, and every block after the first leak
failed for a leak it did not cause.

ObjectRegistry.registries is process-global, so start() now records a baseline
and the check compares against it. start() also restores the timer globals
instead of asserting when a previous block never reached its stop(), which
happens whenever a `before` hook fails and mocha skips the matching afterEach.

build(coverage): give c8 a config it can read, and stop counting unloaded files

.nycrc.yaml was an nyc file. c8 parses JSON only, so it ignored the whole thing:
point c8 at it explicitly and it says "all: false ... is not valid JSON". None of
those excludes, and none of that cwd, had ever applied.

Meanwhile the Makefile passed --all, which reports every file whether or not it
ran: 3103 never-loaded .ts files at 0%, and a headline of 28.35% that measured how
many sources compile to how many outputs. On one package's suite, 945 rows and
6.49% before, 87 rows and 68.43% after.

The config moves to .c8rc.json with the excludes c8 already applied by default, so
the published figure does not move. The old file also excluded whole packages;
reinstating those is worth about 15 points and is left as its own decision.

build(coverage): exclude generated code from the report

_generated_* files and the node-opcua-nodeset-* packages are machine written.
Counting them measures the generator, not the tests: _generated_opcua_types
alone is ~34k lines at 58% in a full run.

test(end2end): make the FEAT-37 at-scale burst survive a slow runtime

Three harness defects that surface as "subscriptions without any Publish
response" under c8:

- the burst was aimed using a timestamp taken before a session's five
  subscriptions were created, so it targeted subscription 1's tick while
  subscription 5 ticked however long the creations had taken;
- the wait loop stopped at `expected` answers, so one subscription answering
  twice ended the wait while a sibling was still in flight;
- a fault is recorded against subscriptionId -1, so it was reported as a
  starved subscription rather than as a fault.

No assertion is weakened: the one-answer-per-subscription property still holds.

fix(leak-detector): pass setTimeout arguments through to the callback

setTimeout(fn, delay, ...args) calls fn(...args). The tracking wrapper forwarded
the arguments to the inner setTimeout but then called fn() with none, so a
caller that passes one received undefined. undici does this for its parser
timeout: a fetch whose timeout fired under the detector threw "Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'deref')" from inside undici.

Also keep generated code in the coverage report: excluding it moves the
published figure by ~4 points, which is a decision about what the number means
rather than a config repair.

build(coverage): add check-c8-ignore, and write the hints in the form c8 reads

c8 acts on a coverage hint only as a single-line block comment carrying next,
next <n>, start or stop. A `// c8 ignore next` is an ordinary comment, so the
line it was meant to exclude was counted as uncovered: 235 hints across 94
files, every one inert, with nothing to say so.

The gate also catches the block spellings that are silently inert, `/* c8
ignore */` with no directive and `end` for `stop`, and --fix repairs the second.
Verified against a fixture where each spelling guards an uncalled function.

fix: re-export types with `export type`, not as values

Fourteen re-exports named a type in a plain `export { }`. tsc has the whole
program and elides them; tsx and esbuild compile one file at a time and
cannot, so the re-export survived and failed to link under ESM with "does
not provide an export named". Five sat in entry points.

build: type-check with isolatedModules

Makes tsc answer the question a single-file transpiler has to answer, so a
type re-exported as a value is an error at build time rather than a link
failure when the suites run.

test(basic-types): pass the namespace to should(), not through it

A module namespace has a null prototype under real ESM, so it never
inherits Object.prototype.should. Under the CommonJS loader it was an
ordinary object and did.

test: load the suites with the tsx ESM hook (FEAT-4)

Every package publishes ESM since FEAT-2, while the suites were transpiled
to CommonJS, so they exercised a translation of the code we ship and
`require` and `import` returned two instances of the same module. Both
gone: the probe now reports one instance.

fix(end2end): import the callable should, not its namespace

`import * as should` gave a namespace whose only key is `default`, so
`should.exist` was undefined and threw inside a read callback before it
could resolve its promise. The test then hung to the 30s timeout. Only
visible under the ESM loader; tsx/cjs papered over it with interop.

test: load root-level mocha runs with the tsx ESM hook

The root config still registered tsx/cjs, so a run from the repo root
transpiled each package's ESM dist back to CommonJS and replaced its
source map: coverage reported dist/*.js where the same suite reports
source/*.ts under the ESM hook. packages/.mocharc.js moved in FEAT-4;
this is the last config that had not.

fix(service-filter): treat an empty select clause browsePath as Good

checkSelectClause fed an empty SimpleAttributeOperand.browsePath into
the TranslateBrowsePath-style browse(), which reports BadNothingToDo
for zero relativePath elements. OPC 10000-4 7.4.4.5 says an empty
browsePath denotes the instance of typeDefinitionId itself, so the
clause is valid. This broke the ConditionId select clause every
Alarms and Conditions client sends, even though delivery already
returned the right value.

Return Good directly once typeDefinitionId has been confirmed to
resolve to a real EventType; an unresolved or wrong-class
typeDefinitionId still fails earlier in the same function.

Adds a test in node-opcua-server/test/test_raise_event.ts covering
both the fixed Good case and the still-rejected unknown-type case.

fix(service-filter): resolve empty-browsePath ConditionId in where clauses

resolveOperand fed an empty SimpleAttributeOperand.browsePath into the
same browse() FEAT-58 fixed on the select side, so a where clause
built on the ConditionId (InList or Equals, as every Alarms and
Conditions client sends) never matched. Share the empty-browsePath
resolution between resolveOperand and extractEventField so evaluation
and delivery can no longer drift apart.

Adds where-clause tests in node-opcua-server/test/test_raise_event.ts.

build(tools): add check-erasable, a gate for Node type stripping

The suite is moving to Node's own type stripping, which erases type syntax
and emits nothing: an enum, a namespace, a parameter property, an angle
cast or an import= is refused at load time with
ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Ten test files were rewritten for it
and nothing stopped the eleventh. Test trees only; source is reached
through its compiled dist and never stripped.

test(runner): add NATIVE_TS mode running on Node's own type stripping

NATIVE_TS=1 replaces the tsx registration with two resolver redirects, so no
import is rewritten and no experimental flag is needed. tsx hands V8 its own
transform of the already-compiled dist/*.js, which defeats c8's source-map
remap and makes the published coverage figure measure compiled JavaScript
rather than the TypeScript a developer can act on.

Test files are adjusted for erasable syntax: parameter properties, enums
rewritten as `as const` objects with a merged type alias, angle-bracket casts,
and should() taking its subject as an argument.

test(server): write the mock queue cast in the erasable form

`<unknown[]>[]` is the angle-bracket assertion, which Node's type stripping
rejects. helper.ts is imported by six specs, so the one cast kept all of them
from loading without a transpiler.

ci(coverage): measure the suite under NATIVE_TS

tsx rewrites a workspace package's compiled dist/*.js and substitutes its own
source map, so c8 never follows the map back to the .ts. A package reached
through its package name is reported as dist, the same package reached by a
relative path is reported as source, and the two sets of counts never merge:
7 packages are counted twice today and 16 only as dist.

Measured on node-opcua-aggregates, same tests, loader the only variable:
dist/aggregates.js 83.94% under tsx, source/aggregates.ts 86.20% without it.

test(schemas): restore the expected generator output

The enums in this file sit inside the template literal that describes what
toTypeScript emits, so they are text, not TypeScript, and never needed the
erasable-syntax rewrite. Converting them changed the assertion instead of the
code under test, and the generator still emits `export enum`.
ci(coverage): do not bail on this measurement branch

fix(runner): register the tsx ESM hooks through their own api

register("tsx/esm/api", ...) installs hooks that never perform the NodeNext
.js -> .ts resolution, so `import "./x.js"` next to an x.ts throws
ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. The CJS hook registered just above runs first and covered
for it, so the tsx path only looked healthy. ("tsx/esm" refuses outright and
asks for --import.)

Found by the FEAT-4 session; repro is a bare register() of either specifier
against any of the repo's .js-spelled TypeScript imports.

test(runner): make native type stripping the default, tsx the fallback

The suite now runs on Node's own stripping unless TSX=1 is set. tsx's CommonJS
hook re-transpiles each package's compiled dist/*.js and substitutes its own
source map, so c8 could not follow the map back to the .ts: the same package
was reported under dist/ when reached by package name and under source/ when
reached by a relative path, and the two never merged. Whole suite, same tests:
79.06% of lines that way, 91.70% without tsx, on an unchanged denominator.

The fallback registers only the ESM hooks. Re-registering the CommonJS one
would reintroduce the defect this replaces.

build: run check:erasable in the lint job

The gate landed unwired because it reported 11 findings until the
NATIVE_TS fixes merged. Both are on master now and it reports clean, so
it can enforce rather than sit there.

test(discovery): count this test's own announcement, not the subnet's

The browser hears every opcua-tcp announcement on the network, so a
parallel suite or another checkout made spyUp fire twice and the run
failed with "expected 2 to equal 1". The spies now filter on a service
name unique to the run.

build(tools): let the ESM gates see bin/

shippedDirsOf excludes bin/ because a package does not publish it, which
left no gate looking at scripts Node runs directly. Three defects sat
there: a `".."` specifier NodeNext cannot resolve, a missing extension,
and two `__dirname` uses in an ES module.

build(tools): stop asking attw about packages with nothing to import

node-opcua-samples was the last baselined package. It declares bin and no
main, types or exports, so attw's "import failed to resolve" was a
category error rather than a defect, and baselining it hid the question
instead of answering it. The baseline is now empty.

fix(address-space): an enumValues entry keeps its description

coerceEnumValues built each EnumValueType from displayName and value
only, so a description passed in the array form of enumValues was
accepted by the type checker and then dropped. The object-map form
already set one, which made the omission easy to miss.

fix(generator): delete the scratch entry point, import schemas as URLs

opcua_code_generator.ts had no references anywhere: not exported, not a
bin, hardcodes one class name and swallows its own errors. The two
dynamic imports on the deprecated schema-literal path now go through
pathToFileURL, since an absolute Windows path reads "C:" as a URL scheme.

build(tools): fail on an import into another package's impl/

FEAT-11 moved the implementation behind impl/ and FEAT-14 published what
downstream needed, so there is a supported name to use instead. Nothing
stopped this repo's own tests and playground taking the internal path,
which is how the deep-import surface accumulated before. The count is
zero today, so the gate starts absolute rather than as a baseline.

test(enum): a benchmark result cannot abort the test runner

The speed comparison ran in a "complete" event handler and Benchmarker.run()
was never awaited, so both a timing inversion and a failed assertion inside a
measured function escaped as unhandled rejections, killing the runner and the
suites still in flight rather than failing one test.

Report through done() instead, and treat a wall clock inversion on a shared
runner as a warning rather than a verdict on the code.

feat(address-space): deleteNamespace, so a namespace can be emptied and reused

A namespace could be populated but never cleanly removed. _deleteNode
threw on DataType and ReferenceType, because their unregister helpers
were never written, and deleting node by node left survivors behind.

deleteNamespace empties one inside a single model-change transaction,
severing only the references that cross out of the namespace, and leaves
it registered and ready to be populated again.

Two fixes it rests on. A DataTypeFactory now chains to the namespaces it
depends on rather than to every namespace loaded before it, so dropping
one no longer leaves unrelated namespaces holding a discarded factory.
And ensureDatatypeExtracted no longer returns early for a namespace that
was emptied and populated again, which would have left its structures
unextracted.

fix(address-space): keep the factory chain positional for now

Chaining a DataTypeFactory to its real dependencies instead of to every
earlier namespace turned out not to be a one-line change, and CI caught
it: constructNamespaceDependency walks values and throws on an
ExtensionObject with a null schema. Being debug-only until now, it never
had to survive the hot path, so calling it on every load broke server
writes with "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'schema')".

Reverted to the shipped behaviour, with the reason recorded where the
dead computation still sits. Hardening that walk and switching the chain
belong together in their own change, with tests for the walk.

deleteNamespace does not depend on it: its 9 tests pass either way. The
cost of leaving it is that deleting a namespace others were chained to
positionally leaves them holding a discarded factory, which
unregisterDataTypeFactory already warns about.

perf(address-space): skip the proof that an unedited nodeset is unedited

Two costs a load pays for nothing, both opt-in or invisible.

Validating a sibling image reads and SHA-256s the whole XML — about
30ms of the ~110ms it takes to replay the standard nodeset — to prove a
file nobody edited has not changed. trustSiblingImages, off by default,
makes the recorded source length against the file size the whole check
and never reads the XML. The schema, trailer and node count are still
verified; what it gives up is precisely an edit that keeps the byte
length identical, which cannot happen to a nodeset a package ships.

And every Variable took its own clock reading, twice — once built, once
given a value. They now share one reading per load, scoped to the
address space being loaded and reference counted, so a write to an
address space that is not loading still gets a real clock. Nodes from
one file now carry one timestamp rather than timestamps microseconds
apart.

perf(address-space): stop the loader reading scanning getters per node

Two internal changes, no behaviour change.

The UAObject constructor asserted on `this.eventNotifier`, a getter that
scans references through getEventSources and getNotifiers — on a node
the loader has just built and whose references it has not wired yet. It
now asserts on the declared flags, which hold the same value at that
point. One standard+di load drops from 10,136 findReferences calls to
6,132, and from 4,898 findReferencesAsObject to 894.

nodeIdOf probed the alias object and then the id map, about 50,000
double lookups per document; aliases are seeded into the map instead.

Timing moves 0-4%, at this machine's resolution limit; the call counts
are the measurable part. Benchmarks that produced them are included.

perf(address-space): decode an image node without probing nineteen absent keys

Two allocations removed from the per-node path of an image load.

References were rebuilt with `map`, allocating a closure per node and
growing the array as it went; a nodeset carries twenty thousand of them,
so the array is sized once and filled in place instead.

The optional scalar fields were copied by asking each node for all
nineteen of them. A node carries a handful, so the loop now walks the
keys the writer actually emitted and keeps the ones that belong.

Proved faithful by the image-versus-XML comparison in TSI1, which
compares every node and every reference rather than counting them.

perf(address-space): answer the three DataType questions in one chain walk

`_getDefinition` asked isSubtypeOf three times — Enumeration, Structure,
Union — and each call walked the supertype chain by filtering the whole
reference list of every node on the way up. isSubtypeOf does memoize, but
its memo is keyed on a counter bumped whenever a HasSubtype reference is
added anywhere, so during a load, which adds thousands, the memo is
discarded before it is ever read.

One walk now answers all three, over subtypeOfObj, which is cached per
node. A standard+DI load drops from 2966 allReferences calls to 236.

The declaration index of the narrowing sweep is keyed on the type node
instead of on a `${nodeId}|${browseName}` string, so a lookup no longer
renders two objects to text and joins them — thousands of times, on hits
as much as on misses.

The benchmarks that produced these numbers are included, one of them a
negative result: NDJSON lines are already parsed the fastest way of four.

casos.name: v12.0.0
casos.body:
This release introduces asynchronous metrics, broadens codec coverage, and adds API and reliability improvements across backend lifecycle handling, sinks, and platform-specific paths.

Quill can now offload both logs and metric samples through the same backend worker, with metric metadata registered up front and each publish call enqueueing only a compact, fixed-size sample record on the hot path.

- Added asynchronous metrics support, including metric registration APIs, `Logger::publish_metric()`, the `METRIC(...)` macro, and backend sink delivery through `Sink::write_metric()`.
- Added an optional `PrometheusSink` and examples for both a custom metric sink and Prometheus-backed export: [custom metric sink example](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/blob/master/docs/snippets/quill_docs_example_metric_publishing.cpp), [Prometheus sink example](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/blob/master/examples/metric_publishing_prometheus.cpp)
- Added per-thread mapped diagnostic context (MDC) support with `Logger::set_mdc()`, `Logger::erase_mdc()`, `Logger::clear_mdc()`, the `%(mdc)` pattern attribute, and `BackendOptions::mdc_format_pattern` for global MDC rendering.
- Added std codec support for `std::variant`, `std::bitset`, `std::complex`, and `std::error_code`.
- Extended `quill/std/Chrono.h` codec support to match bundled fmt's C++20 calendar formatters, including `std::chrono::year`, `month`, `day`, `weekday`, and `year_month_day` when available.
- Added C++20 module support groundwork, including export markers and macro cleanup.
- Switched to native file handles (`CreateFile`/`WriteFile`) on Windows for improved write throughput compared to `FILE*`.
- Added strict `Frontend::create_sink()` and `Frontend::create_logger()` APIs for callers that want duplicate names to fail instead of reusing existing objects.
- Added `CsvWriter::close()` for deterministic logger removal and file closure before backend shutdown.
- Added `BackendOptions::ensure_monotonic_output_timestamps` to correct regular log and metric output timestamps that would otherwise move backwards. Backtrace records keep their original capture timestamps.
- `BackendOptions::cpu_affinity` now supports pinning the backend to multiple CPUs.
- Added a fallback to `fs::absolute` when `fs::canonical` fails on RAM disks. ([#910](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/issues/910))
- Hardened backend, signal-handler, manual-backend, and teardown paths with more robust startup and shutdown behavior.
- Fixed multiple codec, sink rotation, named-argument, queue, and platform-specific edge cases.
- Fixed an infinite loop in the backend when the user-provided `error_notifier` throws. ([#915](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/issues/915))
- Generated a Doxygen tag file for downstream documentation linking. ([#914](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/issues/914))
- Fix rotating sink reopen failure when the disk is full ([#919](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/issues/919))
- Fixes DLL unload on Windows, drain remaining log messages in stop() when backend thread was terminated externally ([#925](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/discussions/925))
- Fixed stale named arguments from a pooled `TransitEvent`. The `named_args` pointer is now consistently `nullptr` for log statements without named arguments instead of occasionally being an empty vector ([#926](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/issues/926))
- `StopWatch` now samples its elapsed time on the frontend at the log call site instead of when the backend formats the message, so logged values no longer include backend latency.
- `RotatingFileSink` in append mode now counts rotated files left behind by previous runs towards `max_backup_files` for all `RotationNamingScheme` values, removing the oldest files on startup when they exceed the limit instead of letting them accumulate across restarts. Previously only the `Index` scheme (and the `Date` scheme for same-day files) recovered existing files, so `Date` and `DateAndTime` files from earlier runs were never cleaned up. Recovered append-mode files are not removed when `overwrite_rolled_files` is set to `false`. ([#930](https://github.com/odygrd/quill/discussions/930))

Use soft rdtsc fallback on 32-bit PowerPC (#911)

Quill's rdtsc helper already avoids __rdtsc() on ARM and PPC64, but
32-bit PowerPC was not included in that guard. On powerpc targets this
falls through to the x86-specific intrinsic and fails with:

  error: '__rdtsc' was not declared in this scope

Treat common 32-bit PowerPC compiler define the same way as PPC64 and
use the existing steady_clock-based fallback.

Signed-off-by: Peter Marko <peter.marko@siemens.com>

fix rotating sink reopen failure when disk is full (#919)

* add rotating sink reopen failure regression test

A disk-full condition could make log rotation fail while reopening the
active log file. That failure left the rotating sink with a null FILE*,
and the next oversized write re-entered the rotation path and uncondi
-tionally called fsync_file(), which reached fileno(nullptr) and
crashed with SIGSEGV.

* fix rotating sink reopen failure when disk is full

* fix rotating sink recovery after failed reopen

Extend codecs and backend event handling

- Extend the backend event path to carry numeric samples

Exception-safety and shutdown fixes

- Drain remaining log messages when the backend thread is terminated externally

Add DINOv3 finetuning for image segmentation (#589)

* Add DINOv3 finetuning for image segmentation

Implements DINOv3 backbone finetuning with DPT decoder for semantic
segmentation of geospatial imagery, addressing issue #250.

Key components:
- DINOv3Segmenter: PyTorch Lightning module with frozen DINOv3 backbone,
  multi-scale feature extraction from intermediate ViT layers, and DPT
  (Dense Prediction Transformer) decoder head
- LoRA support: Optional Low-Rank Adaptation for parameter-efficient
  backbone finetuning without full weight updates
- DPTSegmentationHead: Multi-scale feature fusion with progressive
  upsampling for dense per-pixel prediction
- DINOv3SegmentationDataset: GeoTIFF-aware dataset with rasterio loading,
  configurable number of input channels, and nodata-aware masking
- train_dinov3_segmentation(): End-to-end training function with
  train/val/test splits, early stopping, and model checkpointing
- dinov3_segment_geotiff(): Sliding-window inference on large GeoTIFFs
  with overlap blending via probability-based soft voting and proper
  CRS/transform preservation in output

Supports all DINOv3 model sizes (S/B/L/g) with automatic extraction
layer selection based on transformer depth. Follows existing project
patterns from timm_segment.py for Lightning integration.

* Fix bugs and add batched inference for DINOv3 segmentation

- Fix mock test: handle list n parameter in get_intermediate_layers
  (would crash with TypeError when Lightning is installed)
- Add overlap >= window_size validation in dinov3_segment_geotiff
- Warn when weights_path does not exist instead of silent fallback
- Implement batched window inference using batch_size parameter

- Add tests for overlap validation edge cases
